title: The Last Honest Meal: Why Home Cooking Is Becoming a Radical Act
excerpt: In an economy built on convenience, choosing to cook slowly at home has quietly become a small act of resistance — and self-respect.
body:
Convenience Was Never Free

Every delivery app promises to save you time. What it rarely mentions is what it costs you instead: attention, ritual, and the small daily proof that you can take care of yourself with your own hands.

The Kitchen as the Last Unautomated Room

Most of modern life has been optimized into someone else's algorithm — what you watch, what you buy, who you talk to. The kitchen remains stubbornly analog. No recommendation engine decides how much salt your dal needs. That friction, annoying as it can feel on a tired Tuesday, is exactly the point.

Slowness as Signal, Not Inefficiency

A thirty-minute meal you cooked yourself sends a different signal to your nervous system than a fifteen-minute one that arrived in plastic. It says: I am worth the wait. Over time, that signal compounds into something larger than nutrition — a relationship with yourself that isn't mediated by a screen.

You Don't Need to Cook Every Meal

This isn't a call to abandon convenience entirely — that's its own kind of purity spiral. It's an invitation to notice how rarely you choose slowness on purpose, and what changes when you do, even once a week.
